title: Nobody’s Ghost
subtitle: The Legend of Nine
teaser: The only person who ever heard him coming was six years old. She was standing on the stairs with a candle, and she asked him, very politely, whether he was a ghost.

sections.heading: I. Numbers
paragraphs: The only person who ever heard him coming was six years old.

Everyone else has turned around too late. That was what he was made for. The Hollow Hand made him, out of a boy of four asleep on the canal steps of Ostrel, and the first thing they took from him was his name.

They gave him a number instead. When a child of the Hand died, the number went to the next child off the steps, and nobody had to learn anything new. Nine’s bunk had his number cut into it four times. The first three were scratched out.

The Hand kept its hall in an old rendering house on the tallow wharves, its walls soaked with a hundred years of boiled fat. There the children learned to climb, to pick locks, to walk on the outside edges of their feet, and to crack ash-eggs, clay shells of powder that burst into smoke, and be somewhere else when it cleared. They wore teal-black, the colour of the canals at midnight.
At six, the drops began: nightshade, one drop in each eye every night for a year, until the dark stopped being dark. It turned the eyes red for good. In real darkness, they glowed.

The children had one game, and the masters allowed it because it was useful. You crept up behind someone, touched the back of their neck with one finger, and said, “You never heard me.” If they heard you first, you lost.
Nine never lost.

Twelve never won. She was two years younger, small and freckled, and she hummed when she concentrated, which was always. He spent a winter trying to teach her. Breathe out when you step. Heel down last. Stop humming.
“I’m not humming.”
“You’re humming now.”
One evening on the drying roof, he heard her humming from twenty feet away. He kept his eyes on the canal and didn’t move. A small cold finger touched the back of his neck.
“You never heard me!” She was so pleased she nearly fell off the roof.
“No,” he lied. “I never did.”
She went out on her first job at thirteen and didn’t come back. The masters said she had been heard. By morning there was a four-year-old crying in her bunk, and a fresh scratch on the wood.
Nine never let anyone win again.

sections.heading: II. The Chandler’s House
paragraphs: At sixteen, they sent him to the house of Pieter Kalden, a chandler whose beeswax lit half the churches in Ostrel. A rival had paid for the whole household: the chandler, his wife, the servants and their only child, so that nobody would be left to inherit.

The Hand never sent one knife. It sent a hand: a thumb to go in, and four fingers on the rooftops around the house. If the thumb wasn’t out when the cathedral bell struck the half hour, the fingers went in.

Nine was the thumb. He came in through the skylight. The house smelled of honey, and a nightlight burned in every room. He went down the stairs on the outside edges of his feet, and not one of them creaked.
“Excuse me,” said a small voice.

She was standing on the landing in her nightgown, holding a candle in a brass dish. Six years old, her plait coming loose from sleep. She was looking straight into his red eyes, and she didn’t scream.
“I heard you on the stairs,” she said. “Are you a ghost?”
Nobody had ever heard him on the stairs. He said the first thing that came into his head, which happened to be true. “Yes.”
She considered this. “Whose?”
“What?”
“Ghosts are always somebody’s. Grandmama is in the stockroom. Mama says. Whose are you?”
“Nobody’s.”
She frowned, as though that were a little rude. “What’s your name, then?”
“I don’t have one. I have a number. Nine.”
“That’s not a name. That’s how old my cousin is.” She held out the candle. “You can borrow this. It’s dark on the stairs, and you’ll fall down.”
He looked at the candle, and at the small hand holding it. Then he put the knives away.
When the bell struck the half, four masters would come in, and he could do nothing against four. He could not save a household. He could carry one child.
“Do you want to play a game? It’s called You Never Heard Me. We go out through the cellar, and if nobody hears us, you win.”

She was very good at it. She held her breath all the way down the cellar steps and up the coal chute into the alley, her arms round his neck, the candle still in her fist. It had gone out. At the end of the alley, he looked back.
The cathedral bell struck the half. One by one, the nightlights in the chandler’s windows went out.
She didn’t see. Her face was in his cloak.
“Did I win?” she whispered.
It was a long time before he could answer. “Yes.”

sections.heading: III. The Rendering House
paragraphs: The Hand would come for him before morning, and for her. So he went to them first.
He hid her under a tarpaulin in a coal barge at the Tanner’s Steps and told her the game wasn’t over: not a sound, whatever she heard, until he came back and said her name.
“You don’t know my name.”
“Then tell me.”
“Tilde.”
He said it once under his breath, to keep it safe. Nobody had ever trusted him with a name before.
The masters were waiting in the rendering house, around the long table under its one lamp. Not one of them heard him come in, or bar the street door behind him.

He went to the dormitory first and woke the children one at a time, a finger on the back of the neck, the way you do in the game. “Run,” he told each one, at the canal door. “Don’t come back. Pick a name.”
The new Twelve was five. She held on to his cloak and asked him what name.
“Any one you like. That’s the point.”
Then he went into the hall and stood behind the chair of Master Lusk, who had put the first drops in his eyes.
“Nine ran,” Lusk was saying. “Find him. Bring me the girl. Then bring me his number, and we’ll give it to someone who can use it.”
Nine bent to the old man’s ear. “You never heard me,” he said, and knocked the lamp off the table.

He cracked an ash-egg under his heel. In the smoke, the masters stabbed at each other, and at nothing. By the time it thinned, the fire had found a hundred years of tallow in the walls. He went out through the canal door and dropped the bar behind him. Every master of the Hollow Hand was inside, and not one of them heard it fall.
The fire had burned his cloak to rags at the hem. He didn’t notice until he lifted the tarpaulin. She was lying exactly where he had left her, the dead candle in her fist.
“Tilde,” he said.
She sat up. “I didn’t make a sound. Not even when the bells went.”

sections.heading: IV. Ghosts Always Come Back
paragraphs: It took them five days to walk to the temple at Sennet, high in the hills, where nobody had ever heard of the Hollow Hand.

She rode on his shoulders and named every candle in her father’s shop, in order: tapers, rushlights, church candles, and the fat bayberry ones for midwinter that made the whole house smell green. She called him Nine, since he wouldn’t give her anything else, and decided it was a name after all, if you said it nicely enough.

On the second night she asked where her mother was. He told her the truth, because he didn’t know how to do anything else with her. She cried herself to sleep. She never asked why a ghost had come down her stairs with a knife in each hand. He has wondered every day since whether she knew.
The priest at Sennet was an old woman called Mother Hild, who looked at his eyes, his burnt cloak and the child, and asked nothing at all.
At the gate, Tilde held on to his finger.
“Will you come back?”
“No.”
“Yes, you will,” she said, in the patient voice she had used about her cousin. “Ghosts always come back. That’s what they’re for.”
Then she pressed the candle into his hand, the stub from the stairs, its wick still black.
“For the dark,” she said. “So you don’t fall down.”

His eyes had been made for the dark. He didn’t light it. He walked down the hill with it in his fist and did not look back, because if he had, he would have stayed, and she deserved better than to grow up with the Hollow Hand’s last knife in the house.

sections.heading: V. The Unseen
paragraphs: He fights in the duelling rings now, and the heralds, who have to call him something, call him the Unseen. He comes in hooded, with two short knives and a teal-black cloak burnt to ribbons at the hem, and all anyone sees of his face is two red points of light. He cracks an ash-egg, the smoke takes him, and the next thing his opponent feels is a touch at the back of the neck.
“You never heard me,” he says.
The crowds think it’s a boast. It is the rules of a children’s game, and he has never once lost it, or let anyone win.

He fights because the rings are the only place where a man can come up behind someone and they get up again afterwards. And because it pays. Every coin he wins goes up the river to Sennet: for the roof, for slates and books, for a schoolroom with good windows.
Every year Tilde asks the priest who pays, and the priest says what he was told to say: an old friend of her father’s.

If she ever asks Nine himself, he has a truer answer ready, fourteen years in the choosing: “Someone who owes you.” And if she asks the next question, he will tell her the rest, the stairs and the bell and the nightlights going out, and let her do whatever she likes with it. That is why he has never let her see him.

But once a year he climbs the hill above Sennet at dusk and stands under the old pear tree where the schoolroom light doesn’t reach, and watches Tilde Kalden teach the village children to read. She is twenty. She makes the candles herself, out of beeswax, the way her father did.
Nobody has ever seen him there.
Last summer, when the children had run home, she came out onto the step with a candle and stood looking up into the dark under the pear tree for a long time.
“Goodnight, Nine,” she said, very nicely.
She set the candle on the step and went in.
He waited until her window went dark. Then, for the first time in fourteen years, he came down the hill as far as the step, took the old stub out of his cloak, and lit it from hers.
He carried it all the way down to the river road. He didn’t need it. That was never what it was for.
She is still the only one who ever hears him coming.
